name: Marco Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I'm Marco, 27, I share a house on Canal Street with two friends, Kieran and Joss. I run lathes at Corvel Components, we make brake discs and hubs for a couple of car makers. Been there just under a year, after a few years doing warehouse work and a bit of delivery driving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We do rotating shifts, two weeks of earlies, two of lates. I load rough castings onto two CNC lathes, which are machines that spin the metal and cut it to shape from a program, then I measure the finished discs with a gauge and log it on the tablet. The setter, Big Paul, does the programs and the tool changes, and I'm meant to be learning off him, but I still mess up the offsets and he has to check my work. I like the precision, when a disc comes out exactly right it's satisfying, but the coolant smell gets in your clothes and your hands crack in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, told you so, it's just a fancy autocomplete. In the group chat I'd send a meme about all the tech guys who said we'd be finished. At work nobody would even notice, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use the AI stuff now and then, I got it to help with my CV for Corvel and to explain a page of the lathe manual that made no sense. If it stays like that, a handy tool, my job's the same as it is now, which is hard and badly paid but there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. Keep learning off Big Paul so I can get up to setter one day, which is maybe two more an hour. I'd keep paying off the bike loan, I've got about eight months left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, to be honest. Like, life's still a grind, but it's my grind and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody at work would notice. Is there anything changing there already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's talk about a robot loader for Line 3, an arm that would put the castings on instead of a person. The shop steward, Nadia, says the union's asked what it means for jobs and management's being vague. But that's robots, not the AI stuff, and it's been 'next year' for two years now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money look like month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's half my wage, near enough. Then the bike, phone, food, and whatever's left goes on football and a drink on Fridays. If I get to the end of the month with fifty left I'm happy, which is mad when I say it out loud.

S0.say: He'd say AI turned out to be fancy autocomplete and send a meme about the tech crowd to his group chat. At work, he thinks nobody would notice anything.
S0.think: He sees AI as a handy tool he uses now and then, for his CV or a confusing manual page. If it stays that way his job stays hard, badly paid, but there.
S0.do: Carries on learning from the setter so he can move up in time for a small pay rise. Keeps paying off his motorbike loan, with about eight months left.
S0.feel: Calm, the familiar feeling of a grind he knows.
S0.quote: If I get to the end of the month with fifty left I'm happy, which is mad when I say it out loud.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is relaxed about AI because he's used it and found it modest. The robot loader for Line 3 is the real change on the horizon, but he files it under 'always next year'. Money is tight but he talks about it lightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the union earns its money, making sure the company trains people up instead of just dropping them. I'd back Nadia at any meeting. Online I'd share stuff about the government paying for retraining, because that should be public, not on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think loading castings is the first thing to go, and that's most of my job right now. If I'm still not a setter when it hits, I'm the one who's not needed. But if I can get up to setting or programming, I think I'm alright, there'll still be someone needed to look after the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Corvel offered a course, I'd take it, no question. If they didn't, I'd wait to see what Kieran's cousin does, he did a CNC programming course at the college last year and if it works out for him I'd sign up too. I'd start using the AI more to understand the programs, like asking it what each line of the code does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit uneasy, but it feels like there's a ladder there if I can grab it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs money you don't have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then that's the problem, isn't it. The college one was something like six hundred, and I haven't got six hundred. I'd ask the union if there's a fund, and I'd push for the government to cover it, because that's what should happen anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys on the deburring bench, the ones who've done it twenty years. They're not going to want to learn programming at fifty-five. Nadia would fight for them, but I don't know what they'd end up doing.

S1.say: He'd say this is when the union earns its money, making the company retrain people rather than drop them. Online he'd share posts calling for government-funded retraining.
S1.think: He expects the loading part of his job to go first, which is most of what he does now. If he can move up to setting or programming before then, he thinks he'll be fine.
S1.do: Takes any course Corvel offers; if none, waits to see how a friend's cousin gets on with a college CNC programming course and then follows. Uses AI tools more to understand the lathe programs, and asks the union about a fund for the roughly six-hundred course fee.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, but he sees a ladder he might grab.
S1.quote: I think loading castings is the first thing to go, and that's most of my job right now.
S1.fieldNote: Typical of his style: he'd move once he's seen someone else do it successfully. His politics show up in who should pay, the company or the state, not in resisting the change itself. The course fee is the real barrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that's been allowed to happen. Governments should have been ready, and now millions of us are getting thrown out. I'd be at any protest going, and I'd be loud online about taxing the companies doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished at Corvel in that picture. If a robot can set the lathe and program it too, then even if I'd climbed the ladder it wouldn't matter. Two years isn't enough to get anywhere, I'd just be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all extras straight away, football, Friday drinks, the lot, and I'd ask the bike place if I can pause the loan or sell the bike. I'd go to every union meeting and every protest. If the job went, I'd move back in with my mum and dad in Ashby, which is forty minutes away, and apply for whatever support exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mainly. And angry, because it'd feel like nobody bothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum and dad when you moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad worked at the tyre factory until it shut, so he'd get it. He'd probably say something like, 'Same thing happened to me, son, you just keep going.' But I'd feel like a kid, 29 and back in my old room with the football posters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for whatever support exists. What would you hope for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some kind of basic income, where everyone gets money each month whether they work or not. I know people say it's a fantasy, but if robots are doing all the work, where else is the money going to come from? Either that or it all goes to whoever owns the robots.

S2.say: He'd call it a disaster governments let happen and join any protest. Online he'd argue for taxing the companies that profit.
S2.think: He believes his job would be gone even if he'd moved up, because robots could also set and program the lathes. Two years would leave him scrambling.
S2.do: Cuts football, nights out and other extras immediately and tries to pause the bike loan or sell the bike. Attends union meetings and protests, and if he loses the job moves back to his parents' house and claims support.
S2.feel: Scared and angry that no one prepared.
S2.quote: I'd feel like a kid, 29 and back in my old room with the football posters.
S2.fieldNote: The ladder he saw in the slower picture vanishes here, and that changes his tone completely. His father's factory closure gives him a family script for this. He reaches for collective answers like a basic income, while knowing others call it a fantasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, the government should be paying for people to train for whatever's left. I'd be backing candidates who want to tax the robots. At work I'd say get in the union now, while it still means something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32. If I've learned to program by then, maybe I'm one of the ones who looks after the robots for a while, until they don't need that either. I'm not sure. Nobody really knows what's left at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd watch and see if it's really happening, if Corvel starts bringing in the robot loaders and the AI setters. If it is, I'd do the programming course in year two, even if I have to borrow off my sister. Meanwhile I'd try to put away twenty a week and pay off the bike, so I'm not in debt when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. Isn't that a year lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen people jump on stuff that came to nothing, like Joss with his crypto. I'd rather see it with my own eyes on the shop floor. When the first arm goes in on Line 3 and works, that's when I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would borrowing from your sister mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a nurse, she's sensible, she'd lend it but she'd want it back and she'd ask me every month how the course was going. Which is fair, honestly. It'd make me actually finish it.

S3.say: He'd say five years should be used for government-funded training and back candidates who want to tax robots. At work he'd urge people to join the union while it still means something.
S3.think: He'd be 32 and might, if he's learned programming, be one of those who look after the robots for a while. He admits nobody knows what's left at the end.
S3.do: Watches for a year to see whether robot loaders and AI setters actually arrive at Corvel. If they do, takes the programming course in year two, borrowing from his sister if needed, while saving twenty a week and clearing the bike loan.
S3.feel: Nervous, like waiting for exam results.
S3.quote: When the first arm goes in on Line 3 and works, that's when I'd go.
S3.fieldNote: His waiting is deliberate: he wants proof on the shop floor before spending borrowed money. The extra years turn panic into a plan with a trigger point. He pairs personal steps with political ones, which fits his outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, ten years, there's no excuse now, everybody should get a proper plan. I'd push for free college courses for anyone in a job that's going. I'd probably bore people at the bar about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be alright for most of it, actually. I'd be 37 when it arrives, and by then I could be a setter or even a programmer, and have some savings. The end point still scares me, but ten years is a lot of time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Corvel and try to make setter in the next two years. I'd watch what the people who go first do, and once the programming course has a track record I'd do it. I'd vote every time for whoever's serious about a basic income and retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like the normal kind, like thinking about getting old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the end point change how you think about your own future, beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want to be settled, a place with someone, before it all lands. I don't have a girlfriend right now, but in ten years, I'd want that sorted, so you've got someone, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell your 37-year-old self one thing now, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't wait too long. I know I said I'd wait and see, and I would, but there's a point where waiting is just being scared. I'd tell him, when you see it working, move.

S4.say: He'd say ten years leaves no excuse for not giving everyone a proper plan and would push for free college courses for workers in disappearing jobs. He'd talk about it at the bar a lot.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be fine for most of the decade and could become a setter or programmer with some savings by 37. The end point still scares him, but ten years feels like enough time to build something.
S4.do: Keeps working at Corvel aiming for setter within two years. Waits until the programming course has a proven track record before enrolling, and votes for candidates backing basic income and retraining.
S4.feel: A normal kind of unease, like thinking about getting old.
S4.quote: There's a point where waiting is just being scared. I'd tell him, when you see it working, move.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes him relatively relaxed, because he can see a path through promotion and training. He catches his own tendency to wait and names its risk. A personal wish for a settled relationship surfaced here for the first time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. With the others there's a ladder, even if it's wobbly, but with two years there's nothing to climb. What would help is the government paying for retraining and a basic income while you do it, so you're not choosing between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to be the young one who's still learning. Everyone talks about the older workers, and they've got it hard, but I'm 27 with no skills on paper and no money. I've got the whole rest of my working life to get through, and I haven't even got a proper foothold yet.

headlineQuote: I've got the whole rest of my working life to get through, and I haven't even got a proper foothold yet.
portrait: Marco Gupta is a 27-year-old junior lathe operator at a brake parts plant, still learning from the setter and ending most months with about fifty in hand. He uses AI tools now and then and finds them modest, so the slow pictures leave him calm or only uneasy, with a clear ladder towards setting and programming. He moves once he's seen something work, waiting for proof on the shop floor before borrowing for a course. The fast AGI picture takes the ladder away and leaves him scared and angry, imagining moving back to his parents' house at 29. Throughout, he wants the union and government to carry the cost of retraining and backs a basic income.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because in the slower pictures there's a ladder to climb and in two years there's nothing.
whatWouldHelp: The government paying for retraining and a basic income during it, so he isn't choosing between rent and a course.
